slides.title: But it works on my laptop!
slides.tldr: Code that worked once on your laptop and code that works a thousand times, even on a bad day in production, are two different grades of code.

blocks.body: Ryan writes an endpoint that books a parcel with a courier. He runs it ten times on his laptop and it works ten times. Hover over the marked lines to see where this code breaks on a bad day in production.

marks.tip: No validation. If orderId is missing or the JSON is broken, the user gets a raw 500 error.
Nobody checks whose order it is, so anyone can book a parcel on someone else's order. If the order isn't found, calling a method on null crashes.
No timeout: if the courier is slow, this worker hangs for up to 60 seconds. On failure it returns false, and nothing is logged anywhere.
If an impatient customer clicks twice, the whole path runs twice: two parcels on the same order.

blocks.title: What happened in production in the first week
items: The courier's server slowed down; every worker hung and the whole site went down.
A double click booked two parcels on one order, and the cost was paid twice.
Nobody could tell from the logs which order went wrong.

blocks.title: Home cooking and restaurant cooking
blocks.body: If a dinner for four people at home is a little short on salt, nothing is lost. For 500 guests at a banquet, the cook has to think ahead: what if the gas runs out, what if the meat arrives late, who tastes it before it is served? It's the same recipe, but the preparation is different.
Working is not the same as ready. Production-ready code knows what to do on a bad day.

aside.title: The courier's fault, the store goes down
aside.body: One evening, the courier company's server slowed down. The store's code had no timeout, so every request hung and took over all the PHP workers. The problem was the courier's, yet even browsing products on the store stopped working.

items.meaning: The route where everything goes right: valid input, a good network, nobody clicking twice.
A server process that handles one request at a time. There are only so many of them.

check.q: Ryan's code worked every time on his laptop. Why did it break in production?
check.a: On the laptop only the good-day path ran. Production brings slow APIs, bad input and double clicks, and the code had no preparation for any of them.

slides.title: Production-ready means answering seven questions
slides.tldr: Production-ready code answers seven questions: bad input, failures, repeats, permission, visibility, a way back, and proof.

blocks.body: Before lighting the stove, the restaurant cook asks himself a few questions. For code there are seven. You must be able to **show** the answer to each one in the code. "I think it's fine" is not an answer.

blocks.caption: Seven questions: the cook's preparation and what it looks like in code

cells: What if the input is wrong?
Spoiled meat is sent back at the door
A typed DTO, the Validator, a 422 response
rows.tip: Treat everything from outside with suspicion. Stop bad input at the door so it never reaches the code inside.

cells: A spare propane tank in case the gas runs out
Timeouts, caught exceptions, a clear error
rows.tip: Another service will be slow or down sooner or later. Your code shouldn't wait forever, and it should give the user an answer they can understand.

cells: What if the same job arrives twice?
No guest gets the roast twice
An idempotency key, a unique constraint
rows.tip: Double clicks, retries and network glitches send the same request again and again. The result should stay the same as if it came once.
Being logged in isn't enough. You also need to check whether this user may touch this particular order.

cells: How will we know when it goes wrong?
A note of what went into which pot
rows.tip: In production you aren't sitting in front of the screen. Logs and metrics are your eyes, and a log without context (which order, which user) is blind.

cells: How do we get back if it goes bad?
A substitute dish ready if one is spoiled
A feature flag, a reversible migration
rows.tip: Before shipping new code, know how fast you can switch it off. If one switch does it, the cost of a mistake drops sharply.

cells: What is the proof that it works?
Automated tests for the bad paths too
rows.tip: The answers to the six questions above shouldn't be words. If there is a test for each one, that is proof.

blocks.body: Production-ready means the bad-day paths are written, tested and visible from outside.

aside.body: Input, failure, repeat, permission, visibility, way back, proof: if all seven aren't ticked, the work isn't "done".

items.meaning: Doing something ten times has the same result as doing it once.
Being able to tell what is happening inside by looking at logs and metrics from outside.
Taking a new change out and going back to the earlier good state.

check.q: Which questions do you ask to tell whether a new endpoint is production-ready?
check.a: What happens on bad input, when an outside service breaks, when the request arrives twice; whether permission is checked; whether a failure shows up in the logs; whether it can be rolled back; and whether tests cover all of this.

slides.title: From "works" to "ready": the same endpoint, rebuilt
slides.tldr: The same courier booking, now with validation and permission at the door, and inside it a timeout, an idempotency key and logs with context.

blocks.body: Ryan's endpoint now comes in two parts. The controller only does the door's job: checking input and permission. The real work lives in a service that is prepared for failure and repeats.

marks.tip: CreateShipment is a readonly DTO whose orderId has #[Assert\Positive]. On wrong or missing input, Symfony returns a 422 by itself.
If the order isn't found, no crash, just a clean 404.
The OrderVoter checks that the order belongs to this merchant. If not, 403: you can't touch someone else's order.
If the same order comes in a second time, no new parcel: the earlier tracking code is returned.
Even if two requests arrive at exactly the same moment, the courier sees the same key and creates one parcel (provided the courier's API honors idempotency keys).
timeout: give up if nothing comes back for 3 seconds. max_duration: at most 8 seconds for the whole call.
A log with order_id, so you can find exactly this order's incident later.
Your own exception. A listener turns it into a 503 with a "please try again shortly" message. The customer never sees a stack trace.

blocks.body: A timeout on every outside call, and "what if it arrives twice?" answered for every write. Without both answers, the code doesn't merge.

items: Define a client called `courier.client` under `framework.http_client.scoped_clients` and it autowires as `HttpClientInterface $courierClient`.
A timeout doesn't mean "it didn't happen", it means "I don't know". So on the next attempt, send the same idempotency key.
If you don't want to keep the customer waiting for a slow courier, move the job to a queue with Messenger.

items.desc: All tests, including the bad-path ones
Catch null and type mistakes early
Check that service wiring is correct

check.q: What two protections does the new code have against a double click?
check.a: One: if the tracking code already exists, it returns it. Two: it sends the courier the same per-order Idempotency-Key, so even two requests arriving together create just one parcel.

slides.title: Code review: what to look at, in what order
slides.tldr: A review is not about catching typos: first the purpose and design, then failure paths, security and tests, and names and style last.

blocks.title: Tasting before it is served
blocks.body: In a restaurant kitchen, the head cook tastes the food before it goes to the tables. He doesn't look at how the plate is decorated first. He checks whether the meat is cooked and the salt is right. A code review works the same way: the mistake that would make a guest sick comes first, and the garnish comes last.

blocks.caption: The six steps of a review, from costly mistakes to cheap ones

steps.title: 1. Purpose
steps.body: Read the PR description: what problem, and why this solution?
steps.tip: Before opening the code, know what it is meant to do. Without the purpose, you can't judge whether it is right.

steps.title: 2. Design
steps.body: Is the logic in the right place? Is that new table or dependency really needed?
steps.tip: The costliest mistakes are here. Logic in the wrong place or a wrong data model is hard to change after the merge.

steps.title: 3. Correctness and failure
steps.body: What happens with null, an empty list, a double request, a timeout, a break halfway?
steps.tip: The author has usually thought about the good-day path. The reviewer's job is to raise the bad-day questions.

steps.title: 4. Security and data
steps.body: Permission checks, input validation, whether a migration locks the table.
steps.tip: Tests rarely catch these mistakes, but they do the most damage in production.

steps.title: 5. Tests and visibility
steps.body: Are there tests for the bad paths? Will the logs tell you what went wrong?
steps.tip: Don't just check that a test exists. Check whether it would really fail on wrong code.

steps.title: 6. Readability
steps.body: Names, function size, extra complexity. A linter catches style.
steps.tip: Important, but last. Arguments about whitespace and brackets are a job for machines, not people.

blocks.file: Four kinds of good review comments
blocks.code:
blocker: this HTTP call has no timeout. If the courier is slow, every worker
         will hang. How about adding 'timeout' => 3?

question: if the same order comes in twice, will two parcels get booked?

suggestion (optional): these 40 lines would read more easily as a separate
         private method.

praise: great test for the failure case, exactly the one I was looking for.

marks.tip: blocker = no merge until this is fixed. Give the reason and a proposal along with it, not just "wrong".
A question, not an accusation. The author may or may not have thought of it, and either way a conversation starts.
Label what is mandatory and what is only an opinion, so the author doesn't have to guess.

blocks.body: A review judges the code, not the person, and every objection comes with a reason.

items: Approving with "LGTM" without really thinking about the code.
A 1,500-line PR: nobody reads it carefully. Keep PRs between 200 and 400 lines.
20 comments on names and whitespace, and nobody noticed the missing timeout.
Leaving a review sitting for two days: by then the author has lost the context.
Give style arguments to machines: run php-cs-fixer, PHPStan and ESLint in CI.
Review your own PR first. Half the mistakes get caught right there.

check.q: Why does a review look at design and failure paths before names and style?
check.a: Mistakes there cause damage in production and are costly to change later. Style can be caught by a machine and fixed cheaply at any time.

slides.title: Why learn a second ecosystem
slides.tldr: Know only one language and you mistake its habits for rules. Learn a second one and you can see which ideas are universal principles and which are one framework's conventions.

blocks.body: A cook who has only ever grilled burgers thinks cooking means one hot pan and a quick flip. After a month in a sushi kitchen he learns that all the ingredients can be cut and laid out beforehand, and that habit helps his burgers too. Learning Node.js (or Go, or Java) next to PHP does the same: the principles stay, while the surface and the traps change.

blocks.caption: The same question, answered differently in two ecosystems

cells: Starts fresh, everything is wiped at the end
rows.tip: In PHP-FPM, one request's memory or static data doesn't carry over to the next. In Node the process stays alive, so leaks pile up and global data is shared by everyone.

cells: One thread's event loop takes turns
rows.tip: In PHP a slow call blocks one worker, and when workers run out the site is down. In Node, waiting on I/O blocks nobody, but heavy CPU work stops the entire event loop.
The principle is the same: no network call waits forever. Only the way of writing it changes.
In Node, the error of a Promise left without await isn't caught by catch. For a PHP developer this is a completely new kind of trap.
In both places you commit the lock file, so every machine and production get exactly the same versions.

marks.tip: The same idempotency key: the language changed, the principle didn't.
If there is no response in 3 seconds, fetch cancels itself and throws a TimeoutError. This takes the place of Symfony's timeout option.
Unlike PHP's toArray(), fetch does not throw on a 500 or 404. Without this check, the error page would be parsed as if it were a booking.
One catch covers the timeout, a dropped connection, a bad status and broken JSON. It logs with context, like Monolog's context array, and throws your own error, the same as the PHP version.

blocks.title: What a second ecosystem gives you
items: You can separate principle from convention: the timeout is a principle, `HttpClient` is a convention.
You can review the code of the mobile, frontend or data teams, and speak their language.
You can say which tool suits which job from your own experience, not hearsay.

use: You already have experience running code in production in your first ecosystem.
Your team has services in another language that your code talks to.
avoid: Your first one is still shaky: a second one just adds confusion.
Stopping at syntax: you only learn it by deploying a small service.

aside.body: Know one language and you see from inside it. Know two and you see from above.

check.q: Moving from PHP to Node.js, which principles stay the same, and what do you have to rethink?
check.a: Timeouts, idempotency, validation and logs stay the same. You have to rethink the process model: in Node the process stays alive, so memory leaks, shared state and a blocked event loop are new risks.

slides.title: A week spent speeding up the wrong thing
slides.tldr: Optimize by guesswork and you burn time while the real slowness stays. Measure first, then change.

blocks.body: Ryan's `/api/orders` takes 1.4 seconds. The team decided building the JSON must be the slow part, and spent a week writing a custom serializer. The result? 1.4 seconds became 1.36 seconds. Nobody had once measured where the time actually goes. A week later someone opened a profiler and found that a single query was eating 1.18 seconds, because an index was missing.

blocks.caption: Working from guesses versus working from measurements

columns.title: Optimizing by guess
items: "I think the serializer is slow"
A week of code changes
The real problem is untouched
columns.tip: Even experienced developers guess wrong often, because slowness hides in unexpected places.

columns.title: Optimizing by measuring
items: Open the profiler and read the time breakdown
Add one index, 5 minutes
Numbers in hand before and after the change
columns.tip: Profiler first, then one change, then measure again. The result is clear at once.

aside.title: Knuth's famous line
aside.body: "Premature optimization is the root of all evil," said Donald Knuth. It doesn't mean slow code is fine. It means don't optimize without measuring, because for 97% of the code it's pointless, and you have to find the other 3% first.

check.q: The team made the serializer much faster in a week. Why did it gain so little?
check.a: The serializer was only a small slice of the total (about 90ms). The real time went into one query that nobody measured. Optimizing where the time isn't barely changes the total.

slides.title: Measure, pick, change one thing, measure again
slides.tldr: The optimization loop: measure a baseline, find the biggest slice, change just one thing, measure again; if it didn't help, revert.

blocks.title: The doctor's check-up
blocks.body: If you go in with a stomach ache, a good doctor doesn't just write a prescription. First tests, then the cause, then one treatment, then tests again. A slow app is the same. A **profiler** is the X-ray machine, and the **bottleneck** is where it hurts. Treat everything at once and you can't tell what worked.

items.label: Database query
items.tip: About 84% of the total. A query with no index. This is the bottleneck.

items.label: Serializer
items.tip: Ryan's team blamed this one, but it is only 6%.

items.label: Network and other
items.tip: Database connection, sending the response and so on.

blocks.body: Never optimize without measuring. Take the biggest slice first, one change at a time.

aside.body: Measure first, then change, then measure again.

check.q: If the database query takes 84% of the time, how much does the total drop if you make everything else twice as fast?
check.a: Everything else together is a small slice (about 16%), so doubling its speed cuts the total by 8% at best. Leave the biggest slice alone and the gain is small (Amdahl's law).

slides.title: Symfony Profiler, Stopwatch and EXPLAIN
slides.tldr: The Profiler shows which query took how long in a request; Stopwatch times a piece of your own code; EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows how the database ran a query.

blocks.body: Hunt in three steps. First open the **Symfony Profiler** (`/_profiler`): the Doctrine tab shows the time and count of every query, and the Performance tab shows a timeline. Then put a **Stopwatch** around the suspicious part. Finally, ask the database how it ran the slow query with **EXPLAIN ANALYZE**.

marks.tip: Stopwatch only exists in debug. Making it nullable lets the code run in production without breaking.
Give the event a name and the "app" category, and it shows up as a colored block in the Profiler timeline.
ANALYZE really runs the query and shows the actual time. Plain EXPLAIN only shows an estimate.
Seq Scan means reading the whole table. On a big table it is the most common cause of slowness.
An index matching the WHERE and ORDER BY columns. The column order has to be kept right.

items.desc: The Profiler and the debug toolbar
The call graph and timing of one request

items: EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the query. On an UPDATE or DELETE it changes data, so wrap it in a transaction and ROLLBACK.

items.label: Spotting duplicate queries in the Profiler

check.q: The Profiler's Doctrine tab shows the same kind of query 200 times. What does that point to, and what do you do?
check.a: It signals an N+1 query problem. Cut the count with eager loading (`JOIN FETCH`) or a batch query, then measure again.

slides.title: Spike: a small experiment before a big decision
slides.tldr: A spike is time-boxed, throwaway code that answers one specific question (will this library handle 1 million rows?) with numbers.

blocks.title: The banquet kitchen
blocks.body: Before cooking a new pasta sauce for 500, the cook makes one small pot and tastes it. That pot is the **spike**: one question, a fixed time, then the pot is washed. A mistake costs one pot, not 500 plates. What the cook learned is the result, not the pot.

Without a spike: Ryan's team promises a client "the import takes 5 minutes", then spends three weeks building it with one `persist()` per row. On launch day, with 1 million rows, Doctrine keeps every object in memory, the PHP process hits its memory limit around row 200,000 and dies. The promise is already made and three weeks are gone. A one-day spike (below) shows this on day one, and the fix is a small batch size plus `clear()`.

steps.title: 1. One question
steps.body: For example: will importing 1 million rows take 5 minutes?
steps.tip: When the question can be answered with a number, the result is clear. Not "do we like it?".

steps.title: 2. Box the time
steps.tip: Without a time limit, the spike turns into a project of its own.

steps.title: 3. The cheapest code
steps.tip: The aim is learning. Since you will throw the code away, rushing is fine here.

steps.title: 4. Write down the numbers
steps.tip: The final result is a short note: what we tried, what we measured, what we decided.

steps.title: 5. Throw the code away
steps.tip: If spike code slips into production, it becomes debt that haunts you for years.

marks.tip: hrtime(true) gives monotonic time in nanoseconds, a more reliable measure than microtime.
Run it with different batch sizes and compare the numbers. That is the real work of a spike.

items: Write the result of a spike in a short note: the question, the method, the numbers, the decision. If someone asks six months later, the answer exists.
Run it at real data size (millions of rows), not 100 rows; everything is fast on small data.

use: The answer is unknown and wrong guesses are costly: volume, speed, whether a library fits.
avoid: A quick read of the docs answers it, or the choice is easy to undo later.
You have no way to test at real data size; the numbers would mislead.

check.q: Why do you throw the code away after a spike, and what is the real result?
check.a: The code is rushed, with no tests or structure, so it becomes debt if it reaches production. The real result is what you learned: the numbers and the decision, kept in the note.

slides.title: Six measuring mistakes
slides.tldr: Measuring on small data, looking only at averages, measuring in debug mode, not warming the cache, changing many things at once: in all of these the numbers lie.

blocks.body: Measuring wrongly is worse than not measuring: wrong numbers give you confidence while you walk the wrong way. These are the most common mistakes.

blocks.caption: Measuring traps and the right way

rows.tip: Even a Seq Scan is fast on a small table. The problem shows up at millions of rows.
The average can be 100ms while p99 is 5 seconds; users remember that slow share.

cells: Measuring with APP_DEBUG=1 or in dev
The profiler itself is a load
rows.tip: In dev mode Symfony does extra work and the profiler records every request, so the numbers are inflated.

cells: The cache is cold, so it looks slow
Warm up first, then time the next runs
rows.tip: The first request fills the Symfony cache and the database buffers. Throw it away and time the steady state.

cells: Taking the number from one run
Run several times and take the middle
rows.tip: The OS cache, database buffers and other processes all shake a single measurement.

cells: You can't tell which one worked
One change at a time, measure each time
rows.tip: Change many things together and gains and losses blur. One change should mean one difference in one number.

blocks.body: Production-like data, production mode, several runs, look at p95: only then can you trust the numbers.

items: Micro-benchmarks (like `foreach` versus `array_map`) are often meaningless; in a real app I/O eats the time.
Moving spike code into production "just this once". When the question is answered, throw the code away.

check.q: The average response time is 120ms, yet users say the app is "slow". What do you look at?
check.a: p95 and p99, because the average hides the slow share. Perhaps 1% of requests take 4 seconds, and that is what users remember.

slides.title: Facing 500 files on day one
slides.tldr: Read an unfamiliar codebase file by file and you get lost. The fast way is to pick one entry point and follow one job all the way through.

blocks.body: Sarah joins a new company. The project has more than 500 PHP files, and her first task is: "Refund emails aren't going out when a payment fails. Have a look." She starts reading `src/` alphabetically, from the first file. Three hours later she has read 20 files, her head is heavy, and she still doesn't know where the refund code lives.

blocks.caption: Sarah's first approach versus the experienced way

columns.title: Reading file by file
items: Alphabetically, start to finish
Understand everything, then work
20 files in three hours, no idea where
Tired and confused
columns.tip: Code isn't written in alphabetical order; the order of the files and the order of the work are different things.

columns.title: One job from an entry point
items: Find the entry point (route/command/handler)
Follow one request to the end
5 files in 15 minutes, a clear path
Close to the answer to the question
columns.tip: Read only the files that the refund path passes through.

aside.body: A codebase isn't a book to read from the start; it is a city to learn by its routes. Main roads first, side streets later.

check.q: Why didn't Sarah's read-every-file method work?
check.a: The order of the files isn't the path of the work. In three hours she read files that aren't on the refund path. Following one job from an entry point brings in only the files you need.

slides.title: Find the entry points, then ride one bus to the end
slides.tldr: Entry points are routes, console commands, message handlers, event listeners and the scheduler. Follow one request from an entry point to the end and the whole structure starts to make sense.

blocks.title: Bus routes in an unfamiliar city
blocks.body: Arrive in Chicago for the first time and wander the side streets and you will get lost. Instead, learn the **main roads** (the entry points), then board one bus and ride it **all the way** from the northern edge of town to downtown (follow one request). Each stop on the way is a file: the router, the controller, the service, the database. Know one route and you start to understand the shape of the city.

blocks.caption: The stops one Symfony request passes through

nodes.label: public/index.php
nodes.tip: The only front door for web requests. The Kernel starts up from here.

nodes.label: Router
nodes.tip: Looks at the URL and decides which controller runs. `debug:router` shows exactly this list.

nodes.label: Controller
nodes.tip: Takes the user's request and calls a service. Start reading from here.

nodes.label: Service
nodes.tip: The business rules live here. Most of your questions are answered here.

nodes.label: Doctrine / DB
nodes.tip: Reading and writing data. Entities and repositories live here.

nodes.label: JSON response
nodes.tip: The result goes back to the browser as JSON.

edges.label: The request comes in and goes to the Router
The URL is matched and a controller is chosen
The controller hands the job to a service
The service reads or writes data
The result goes back as JSON

blocks.title: The entry points of a Symfony app
items: HTTP route: a controller with `#[Route]`
Console command: `#[AsCommand]`, called from cron
Message handler: `#[AsMessageHandler]`, fed from a queue
Event listener: `#[AsEventListener]`, runs when something happens
Scheduler: `#[AsSchedule]`, clock-driven jobs
Make the question specific: "When does the refund email go out?" Then you can also work backwards from the email-sending code, asking who calls it.
At each stop ask one thing: what does this file take in, what does it return, and who does it call?

check.q: To find out why the refund email isn't sent, which two ways can you start?
check.a: From the front: follow the refund route or command forward. Or from the back: find the email-sending code and see who calls it (a handler or a listener). Both are the two ends of the same path.

slides.title: Symfony tells you itself: the debug commands
slides.tldr: `debug:router`, `debug:container`, `debug:autowiring`, `debug:event-dispatcher`, `debug:messenger`: get a list of the app's structure without reading any code.

blocks.body: With Google Maps in an unfamiliar city, nobody wanders around looking for the road. Symfony's `debug:*` commands are that map: which URL goes to which controller, which service depends on what, who is listening to which event, who handles which message. Run these first, then open the code.

cells: Which controller does this URL run?
rows.tip: A list of all routes with path, method and controller. For one route, `debug:router app_refund` gives the details.

cells: What does this service get, and from whom?
rows.tip: Shows the service's class, its configuration, tags and aliases.
Search by name and you get the interfaces and classes that can be autowired.
The listeners in priority order. It shows which code runs before and after the request.
For each bus, which handler exists for which message.

blocks.code:
php bin/console debug:router --show-controllers | grep -i refund
php bin/console debug:container 'App\Service\RefundService'
php bin/console debug:event-dispatcher App\Event\RefundIssued
php bin/console debug:messenger
php bin/console list app          # the project's own console commands
php bin/console debug:config security access_control

marks.tip: Use grep to filter just the refund routes. See which controller and which method.
Which listeners run when RefundIssued happens (sending the email is probably here).
Commands called from cron or the background are entry points.
One listener answers Sarah's question without reading any code: the refund email is sent in SendRefundEmailListener. Now open that one file.

items.desc: Twig functions, filters and template paths

check.q: When a refund finishes, which listeners run? How do you find out without reading the code?
check.a: Run `php bin/console debug:event-dispatcher App\Event\RefundIssued`. Every listener on that event comes out, in priority order.

slides.title: Tests and git history: the code's written memory
slides.tldr: Tests tell you what the code is supposed to do; git blame and log -S tell you why it is this way and who knows it. Run it as well and you can be sure.

blocks.body: Code tells you *what* is happening, but not *why*. The answer to "why" is in two places: the **tests** (the behavior the code is meant to have) and the **git history** (who changed what, when and for which reason). And when you doubt what the code does, the most honest answer is to run it and see.

blocks.code:
# read the tests to get a list of behaviors
php bin/phpunit --testdox --filter RefundService

# which files change the most (a hint of risk and complexity)
git log --since='6 months ago' --name-only --pretty=format: | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

# who wrote this line, and why
git blame -L 40,60 src/Service/RefundService.php

# the commit where the word `retryCount` appeared or disappeared
git log -S'retryCount' --oneline -- src/

# who knows this area best
git shortlog -sn HEAD -- src/Billing

marks.tip: --testdox turns test names into plain language: "refund fails when already refunded". It is a living document of behavior.
The files that change most often are where bugs and complexity pile up.
Get the commit from blame, then look for the "why" in the commit message and PR with `git show <hash>`.
Pickaxe (-S): when a word was added or removed. The answer to a baffling "why is there a retry here?" is often found this way.

items: Write or change a small test and see: if changing something scares you, that shows where the code has dependencies.
Use Xdebug or `dump()` to look at values in the middle of a request; a value is more trustworthy than a guess.
Don't take a commit message or comment as truth: the code may have changed while the comment stayed old. The code has the last word.

check.q: You see a strange `sleep(2)` in the code. Which git commands do you use to find out why it is there?
check.a: `git blame` to get the line's commit, then `git show` or `git log -S"sleep(2)"` to see when it was added and read the reason in the commit message.

slides.title: Draw a one-page map
slides.tldr: Write down what you have understood: entry points, main services, where data lives, outside dependencies. Drawing your own map is what proves you understand.

blocks.body: Draw by hand what you have understood. Wherever you get stuck while drawing is a gap in your understanding, and the next question lives there. The map doesn't need to be big; boxes and arrows on one page are enough.

blocks.caption: Five steps to draw the map

steps.title: 1. Entry points
steps.tip: Put everything that feeds work into the system on the left.

steps.title: 2. Main services
steps.tip: Pick the 3-5 most-called classes, not all of them.

steps.title: 3. Data
steps.body: Which tables, which caches, which files
steps.tip: Mark where the truth is kept (the source of truth).

steps.title: 4. Outside dependencies
steps.tip: Failures happen most here. Draw them in a different color.

steps.title: 5. Write the questions
steps.body: A list of what you haven't understood
steps.tip: The questions beside the map are your preparation for asking a colleague, better than asking unprepared.

blocks.code:
entry:    POST /api/refunds (RefundController)    cron: app:refund:retry
core:     RefundService -> PaymentGateway, RefundRepository
data:     refunds (Postgres), idempotency key (Redis)
outside:  Stripe gateway (retried on failure), Mailer
events:   RefundIssued -> SendRefundEmailListener  <-- the email is sent here
question: does RefundIssued go through a queue, or is it direct?

marks.tip: This one line answers Sarah's real question: the email is sent in a listener.
Write down the question you still can't answer; it is the reason to run debug:messenger next.

blocks.body: Read code with a question, from an entry point, one request to the end, and draw what you learn.

items: Starting to change code before you understand it. First the map and one small test, then the change.
Taking names and comments as truth. A `PaymentService` may really only send emails; check by running it or with the debug commands.

items.label: Turning the map into lasting documentation

check.q: While drawing the map you can't decide where one arrow goes from and to. What do you do?
check.a: That is exactly the gap in your understanding. Follow one request from there, or run a debug command, then draw the arrow and cross the question off.
